meaning: 'The one who sees clearly' (from δέρκομαι, to see)

pronunciation.approximation: DRAH-kone, stress on the first syllable with a long final ō.
pronunciation.note: Greek δράκων derives from the aorist root of δέρκομαι, "to see clearly" — the dragon is etymologically "the sharp-sighted one," the watcher. The circumflex in Drákōn marks the long ō of the -ων stem; the macron-only Drakōn is the scholarly fallback. The long ō belongs to the nominative singular alone; the oblique stem (drakontos) carries a short o — the macron preserves the nominative's lengthened vowel.

domains.title: The Watcher
domains.subtitle: Guardian Serpents, Spring Wardens, and the Sown Teeth
domains.lead: Drákōn is not the fire-breathing hoard-guard of medieval romance but the Greeks' older idea: the enormous serpent that guards — a spring, a tree, a golden fleece, a goddess's shrine. His name comes from the verb "to see": the dragon is the one who never blinks.

cards.name: The Unsleeping Gaze
cards.desc: From δέρκομαι, "to see" — the dragon's defining power is vigilance, not flame.

cards.name: Python
cards.desc: The earth-serpent of Delphoi slain by Apóllōn, whose rotting gave the site its old name, Pythō.

cards.name: Ladon
cards.desc: The hundred-headed warden of the Hesperides' golden apples, coiled in the sky as Draco.

cards.name: The Sown Teeth
cards.desc: Kadmos killed the Ismenian dragon and planted its teeth — an armed harvest, the Spartoi, sprang up.

symbols.name: The coil
symbols.meaning: The guarding embrace; energy held in reserve around the treasure

symbols.name: The spring
symbols.meaning: What the dragon always guards — water, the earth’s own wealth

symbols.name: The teeth
symbols.meaning: Violence sown into the ground, sprouting as civil strife

symbols.name: The hundred heads
symbols.meaning: Ladon’s answer to the problem of sleeping on duty — Hesiod calls him “terrible, with a hundred voices” (Theogony 333): a warden built so that some head is always awake

symbols.name: The windsock (draco)
symbols.meaning: The hollow bronze serpent standard of Late Roman cavalry, its gaping mouth howling in the wind — the watcher turned into an army’s voice

mythology.lead: Every Greek dragon is a threshold made flesh: kill one and a sanctuary, a city, or a marriage becomes possible — which is why the founders of cities are all, sooner or later, dragonslayers.

myths.title: Apóllōn and Python
myths.text: The Homeric Hymn to Apollo (300–374) tells how the young god, still beardless, sought a site for his oracle and found the spring at Delphoi guarded by a great she-dragon — Typhaon’s nurse, they said, a plague on the flocks and fields of the people. From a hundred paces Apóllōn drew his silver bow and shot; the shaft transfixed her, and she writhed in the dust, gasping out her great breath. Then the god, master of the moment, mocked: “Now rot (pytheu) here upon the fruitful soil — no more will you be a bane to my parishioners.” From the rotting came the old name of the place, Pythō, and of its prophetess, Pythia; the god’s temple was raised beside the spring his arrow had freed. The myth means sanctuary and monster are one package in Greek religion: a god wins his holy place by killing what guarded it — the oracle’s authority is a dragon’s death certificate.

myths.title: Kadmos at the Spring
myths.text: Sent from Phoenicia to find his sister Europa, Kadmos followed an oracle to a cow that would show him where to found a city. Where the cow lay down, the Ismenian spring flowed — guarded by a dragon, offspring of Árēs himself, which killed Kadmos’ men as they drew water. Kadmos hurled a rock that crushed the serpent’s head, then, on Athēnā’s counsel, sowed half its teeth in the plain. Armed men, the Spartoi, the “Sown,” rose from the furrows and at once fell to killing one another, until five remained — the ancestors of Thebes’ proudest houses. Kadmos did penance to Árēs for a year for the death of the god’s son, and the Theban king-list ever after carried the serpent’s blood. The myth means a city is founded on a killing that must be paid for: the polis begins as a debt, and its nobles are sprung, literally, from a dragon’s teeth.

myths.title: Ladon of the Hesperides
myths.text: Beyond Atlas, at the western edge of the world, stood the garden of the Hesperides, where a tree bore golden apples that Gaia had given Hēra at her wedding. Hesiod (Theogony 333–336) calls its guardian a coiling dragon “terrible, with a hundred voices,” offspring of Phorkys and Ketō — Ladon. Hēraklēs’ eleventh labor took the apples: finding the hundred-headed warden unwinnable by force, he sent Atlas for the fruit (or, in the second account, killed Ladon with an arrow) and carried the apples back through the world. Later stargazers set the dragon among the stars as Draco, coiled forever around the north celestial pole — the one constellation that never sets. The myth means the Greeks hung their monsters in the sky to be outlasted nightly by the turning world: even eternity, in their astronomy, is a guard-duty.

myths.title: The Kolchian Warden
myths.text: At the world’s eastern edge, in Árēs’ grove at Kolchis, the Golden Fleece hung in a sacred oak, watched by a dragon that Apollonius describes as vast as a fifty-oared warship — and which never closed its eyes in sleep: the sleepless warden made perfect. No hero could fight it. Mēdeia, priestess and granddaughter of the Sun, did what force could not: her song and her pharmaka — the charm of sleep — drenched the guardian; its great head drooped, its coils loosened, and Iásōn took the fleece from the tree. Ovid (Metamorphoses 7.149–158) keeps the telling detail that Mēdeia herself wept over the sleeping beast she had enchanted. It is the rare Greek dragon defeated not by the spear but by knowledge — by the very intelligence the Greeks called mētis. The myth means the Greeks knew some thresholds open only to the pharmakon: the warden that cannot be beaten can still be sung to sleep.

lore.syncretism: The Roman army adopted the draco — a hollow serpent standard with streaming windsock — from Sarmatian and Dacian cavalry, and Late Roman legions marched under dragons centuries before European heraldry claimed them. Through Latin draco the Greek watcher became the medieval dragon: hoard-guard, maiden-taker, and finally the saint-slaying beast of George and Margaret. The constellation Draco still turns around the pole, Ladon's image fixed in the sky.
lore.culturalLegacy: Every modern "dragon" is his descendant, filtered through Latin and the Middle Ages; yet Greek dragons remained serpents — wingless, earthbound, water-tied — which is why scholars still correct the fire-lizard image. In physics and computing the name lives quietly: Draco the constellation, dragon curve fractals, and "chase the dragon" idioms all pullulate from the Greek root of the watcher who never sleeps.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Drákōn guards what cannot be owned: springs, trees, thresholds. The Greeks knew that every treasure worth having is held by something that watches — and that the hero's real labour is rarely the killing but the seeing: understanding what the dragon was protecting, and why.

Every field still keeps its dragons: the unslept watcher at the edge of the mapped world, guarding the one thing the mapmaker most wants. The Greeks' honesty was to leave the watcher a reason — the spring, the tree, the fleece are never worthless — and their warning was that the slaying is never free: Kadmos founds Thebes on a dragon's grave and pays for it in generations. To name the guardian is to ask the oldest question of ambition: what does this treasure cost, and who was keeping it, and why?

lore.archaeology: Greek dragons are text-and-image creatures: the finest evidence is vase painting, where Python, Ladon, and the Kolchian warden appear as bearded, crested serpents from the 6th century BCE onward — a Ladon on an Apulian vase in Naples shows the many-coiled form most clearly. The dragon's civic role is epigraphic: Thebes' founding myth was official city ideology, and Athens kept a sacred snake on the Acropolis (the "guardian of the citadel" of Herodotus 8.41) as a living drakōn of the polis.
lore.cult: No one built an altar to the drakōn — the word names a class of guardian monsters, not a god with a temple — but serpents lived inside Greek cult at every level. Athens kept a sacred snake on the Acropolis, the 'guardian of the citadel,' fed a monthly honey-cake until the priestess reported it gone on the eve of Salamis (Herodotus 8.41). The Ismenian spring at Thebes, where Kadmos killed the warden, became the sanctuary of Apóllōn Ismenios. Every Asklepieion kept harmless snakes whose touch was therapy, and the Pythia took her title from the rotting of Pythō. Rome, finally, marched under the draco, a hollow bronze serpent standard howling at the head of the column. The honest summary: the dragon itself was never worshipped — but the threshold it guarded always was.
lore.iconography: The Greek dragon is a snake and proud of it — enormous, bearded, sometimes crested, and wingless before the Roman period. Archaic painters set the type: Pythō as a great coiling serpent at the spring, Kadmos' Ismenian warden rearing from its cave, and from the sixth century BCE the scenes multiply on Corinthian and Attic black-figure. The clearest ancient Ladon survives on a fourth-century Apulian krater in Naples, the Hesperides' guardian drawn as a mountain of coils with a hundred heads' worth of menace in a single body; South Italian vase painting of the same century gives the type its baroque final form, all crests and loops. Roman art breaks the rule and adds wings and legs, and the constellation Draco coils permanently around the pole. The medieval west re-imaged the beast entirely — fire, hoard, maiden — but the Greek watcher never needed any of it: the coil and the open eye were the whole portrait.
lore.reception: Latin draco carried the watcher west, and the west rebuilt him in stages. The Physiologus made the dragon the largest of land-beasts and the devil's standard-bearer; the medieval bestiaries copied the file; the Golden Legend handed his scaled heirs to the saints. Norse and Germanic poetry fused him with the older worm — Fáfnir hoards gold in the Eddas, and Beowulf dies by a barrow-drake that is half Greek watcher, half northern wyrm. Romanesque stone pinned him at church doors as evil in sculpture, and the Roman cavalry standard survives, popular tradition insists, in Wales's red dragon, Y Ddraig Goch. Renaissance naturalism tried to file him as zoology — Aldrovandi's Serpentum et draconum historiae (1640) treats him soberly as a subject of inquiry. Nineteenth-century philology recovered the Greek core: δράκων from δέρκομαι, 'the sharp-sighted one,' a guardian defined by watching. Tolkien's Smaug, scholarly to his last scale, reassembled the medieval fire-drake from the same sources — watcher, hoard, and the price of the killing.
